title: Isolate CLI process tests from personal configuration
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:01 -->

**Milestone:** v0.1 follow-up
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

Make the existing deterministic CLI checks give the same result on a clean machine and a developer machine with Schway configured. This repairs an observed verification defect; it does not rebuild basic configuration.

## Existing behavior and problem

The baseline CLI is supposed to load user-global configuration before project and CLI overrides. That behavior is correct. The process-test helper, however, inherits the real user's home while stripping only the Anthropic/OpenAI key variables. At audited revision 875055e, the machine's global configuration selected an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with required authentication. Three assertions therefore observed 'Missing API key for OpenAI-compatible endpoint' instead of their expected missing Anthropic key or missing base URL. The full suite reported 348 pass / 3 fail; the isolated process-test suite reproduced 5 pass / 3 fail.

## Prerequisite contract

No prerequisite implementation is needed. Existing CLI argument/configuration and credential resolution behavior is the contract under test.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Give each process-test case an explicit temporary user-state root, empty unless the case intentionally writes a fixture. Pass that location through the child process environment; leave the invoking user's actual configuration and sessions untouched.

2. Make environment construction explicit: keep runtime/executable lookup necessities, remove ambient provider credentials and Schway-affecting settings, then apply per-test overrides. Tests that need configuration create it themselves.

3. Retain the production precedence defaults < global < project < runtime. Fixing this by disabling global configuration in the real CLI, changing the default provider, weakening assertions, or skipping failing cases does not satisfy this ticket.

4. Retain the existing project-dotenv assertion: entering a project containing a provider key must not silently load that key. Explicit env-file behavior remains a separate intentional input.

5. Exercise both a clean temporary user root and a controlled conflicting compatible-provider configuration. An intentionally configured subprocess must still respect its fixture, proving isolation did not break production configuration.

6. Add a sentinel outside each fixture and verify the harness did not create sessions or modify configuration there. Ensure failed setup and assertion paths clean up temporary state.

## Scope boundary

Test fixtures and subprocess test setup only. No new config features, authentication methods or provider behavior.

## Implementation constraints

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
- Schway owns the loop, session engine, context/compaction and tool scheduling. Provider SDKs are protocol clients with automatic retries disabled; core contracts use native conversation types.
- Keep core independent of OpenTUI and provider wire types. Headless execution must not load the TUI; only selected providers and explicitly enabled executable extensions load.
- Resolve tool-relative paths from the canonical primary workspace root (nearest Git root, otherwise launch cwd). Keep runtime events separate from durable semantic session records.
- Document newly exported functions/types with a one-line TSDoc contract. Preserve bounded model-facing output, exactly one result per accepted call and existing credential redaction.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Default invocation without credentials | Actionable missing Anthropic key, nonzero exit, empty stdout. |
| Compatible selection without endpoint | Missing base URL regardless of the developer's real configuration. |
| Conflicting fixture explicitly selected | Compatible fixture is honored; no contact with a paid service. |
| Project dotenv with a fake secret | No automatic credential loading and no secret in output. |
| Full validation | Focused process suite and full bun test pass; bun run typecheck passes. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Use isolated temporary user configuration and session storage for every CLI subprocess test; retain only explicitly required environment values.
- [ ] Regression coverage installs a conflicting global compatible-provider configuration in a controlled fixture and proves default-provider, missing-base-URL, and dotenv assertions remain independent of the real user's files.
- [ ] Prove subprocess tests neither read nor write real user sessions or credentials and make no paid provider calls.
- [ ] Run the focused CLI process suite and the full Bun test/typecheck checks successfully. Baseline evidence: 348 pass, 3 fail; focused suite 5 pass, 3 fail at revision 875055e.
- [ ] All required behavior and verification scenarios above are covered, including failure/cancellation cases relevant to this slice.
- [ ] User-facing commands/configuration and public contracts introduced by this issue are documented with a runnable example where applicable.

## Completion evidence

Report the implemented user path, relevant checks with observed results, and any remaining limitations. A fixture success does not count as live-provider or human dogfood evidence. Label any required external evidence not run as pending. Do not mark a required failed or pending acceptance item as passed.

## Blocked by

None (can start immediately).

title: Discover and invoke project and global Agent Skills
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:03 -->

**Milestone:** v0.2
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

Users can list local/global skills and explicitly invoke a skill from the interactive editor or a headless prompt, with its instructions reaching the next real model request. Scope: spec sections 45–48, 72, 90.

## Existing behavior and problem

The baseline already assembles environment and scoped project instructions separately from durable messages. It has a fixed slash-command parser and all seven coding tools, but no skill discovery, activation or listing. Add the Agent Skills capability as a complete user-invoked path first. Package skills and model-directed activation are separate later integrations.

## Prerequisite contract

Use the existing context preparation, user-message submission and command-dispatch seams. Export a small discovery/activation service usable by both entry modes and by later model activation; renderer types stay out of it.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Discover project-local and user-global skill directories using the standard SKILL.md convention. Parse the standard name/description and supported invocation metadata, including disable-model-invocation. Keep source identity and the canonical resource base with each discovered skill.

2. Project-local definitions override user-global definitions of the same name. Ambiguous names within one precedence level are explicitly diagnosed and unavailable for invocation; filesystem enumeration order must not choose a winner.

3. At startup expose metadata only. The available-skills context names each eligible skill and how to invoke it without embedding every body. User-only skills remain visible to the user even though they are not model-activatable.

4. Provide /skills and /<skill-name> [arguments] in the TUI. Accept the same explicit skill invocation as a headless prompt. A command-only listing must not call a model. Built-in command names are reserved; explain collisions rather than silently overriding commands.

5. On invocation, read and validate the selected body, attach it as active-skill dynamic context before the next model request, and pass trailing arguments as user input with their meaning preserved. Referenced scripts/assets are available by skill-relative location and are read only when requested.

6. Activation is scoped to the submitted user turn, including all model/tool rounds and automatic compaction in that turn. Clear it on completion, failure or cancellation; a later ordinary turn or resumed session starts without an active body. Durable user invocation text may remain, but full body copies are not appended repeatedly.

7. A malformed skill reports source and reason while unrelated valid skills remain usable. A missing or unreadable body fails that invocation without starting an uninstructed model turn. Bound loaded content using an explicit documented limit and report oversize failure rather than silently truncating instructions.

## Scope boundary

Local/global skill discovery and explicit invocation. No npm package resolution, workflow sequencing or model activation tool in this ticket.

## Implementation constraints

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
- Schway owns the loop, session engine, context/compaction and tool scheduling. Provider SDKs are protocol clients with automatic retries disabled; core contracts use native conversation types.
- Keep core independent of OpenTUI and provider wire types. Headless execution must not load the TUI; only selected providers and explicitly enabled executable extensions load.
- Resolve tool-relative paths from the canonical primary workspace root (nearest Git root, otherwise launch cwd). Keep runtime events separate from durable semantic session records.
- Document newly exported functions/types with a one-line TSDoc contract. Preserve bounded model-facing output, exactly one result per accepted call and existing credential redaction.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Project/global duplicate | The project body reaches the actual prepared request; global body does not. |
| Same-level ambiguity or built-in collision | Explicit diagnostic and no arbitrary invocation. |
| Progressive loading | Unused bodies/resources are never read or injected; explicit activation loads only its body. |
| Real-loop invocation | Scripted model sees body plus arguments alongside project instructions; raw session contains no repeated body. |
| Lifecycle and errors | Subsequent normal turn, resume, cancellation, missing body and malformed metadata behave as specified. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Discover standard skill directories from project and user-global locations; validate name, description and invocation metadata with actionable diagnostics.
- [ ] Project skills override global names; same-precedence duplicates are reported explicitly. Built-in command collisions never silently shadow core commands.
- [ ] Load metadata at startup, full body only on explicit activation, and referenced resources only on demand, resolving resources relative to their skill.
- [ ] Implement skill listing and direct slash invocation including arguments; honor user-only invocation metadata and retain ordinary prompt behavior.
- [ ] Scripted real-loop/controller tests prove actual prompt content, precedence, missing/malformed skills and lazy loading. Update obsolete v0.1 absence guards only for the new skills surface, retaining architectural invariants.
- [ ] All required behavior and verification scenarios above are covered, including failure/cancellation cases relevant to this slice.

title: Activate skills from model requests with a defined lifecycle
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:04 -->

**Milestone:** v0.2
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

The model can activate eligible skills when needed, while explicitly user-only workflows remain user-controlled. Active skill context behaves predictably across turns, compaction and resume.

## Existing behavior and problem

The prerequisite supplies metadata discovery, project-over-global precedence, explicit slash invocation, and a body loader with a canonical resource base. Its activation lasts for one submitted user turn and is dynamic context rather than repeated durable body text. Extend that same service so a model can activate eligible skills; do not create a second loader or different precedence.

## Prerequisite contract

Requires discovered entries with canonical identity, invocation eligibility, resource base, validated body loading and turn-scoped activation from explicit skill support. These capabilities are described here; the blocker link is scheduling metadata.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Expose a validated native activation operation to the model, named activate_skill, accepting a discovered skill name. Register it through the existing tool contract so the request/result path is visible, cancellable and testable.

2. Only skills without disable-model-invocation=true are eligible for model activation. Check eligibility again at execution; hiding a name from metadata alone is not enforcement.

3. Successful activation makes the body available in active-skill context on the next model request within the same user turn. Return a short confirmation as the tool result instead of a full duplicate body.

4. Maintain one active skill at a time. Activating a different skill replaces the earlier active body; activating the same identity again is idempotent. Use exclusive execution for activation so concurrent tool batches cannot race the selected context.

5. Explicit user invocation can activate a user-only skill. Model attempts to replace it still follow eligibility for the target skill; they cannot invoke another user-only workflow through aliases or resource paths.

6. Keep the active body available across pressure/overflow compaction within the turn. Completion, cancellation, error, new session and resume clear active state. On a resumed conversation a model or user may explicitly reactivate; historical invocation messages alone do not reactivate code or instructions.

7. Unknown names, disabled invocation, changed/unreadable bodies and cancellation produce bounded tool errors without damaging sibling results or silently clearing a previously valid active skill.

## Scope boundary

Model-driven skill activation and shared lifecycle. Workflow ordering, plans and orchestration stay in skill instructions.

## Implementation constraints

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
- Schway owns the loop, session engine, context/compaction and tool scheduling. Provider SDKs are protocol clients with automatic retries disabled; core contracts use native conversation types.
- Keep core independent of OpenTUI and provider wire types. Headless execution must not load the TUI; only selected providers and explicitly enabled executable extensions load.
- Resolve tool-relative paths from the canonical primary workspace root (nearest Git root, otherwise launch cwd). Keep runtime events separate from durable semantic session records.
- Document newly exported functions/types with a one-line TSDoc contract. Preserve bounded model-facing output, exactly one result per accepted call and existing credential redaction.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Eligible activation | Actual next request contains the selected body and normal project context. |
| User-only target | Model operation returns an error; explicit slash invocation succeeds. |
| Replacement and duplicate activation | Only one body is active; repeated same-skill activation creates no repeated context. |
| Compaction/resume | Compaction during the turn retains active context; persisted/resumed history does not reactivate it. |
| Concurrent calls and failure | Exclusive activation is ordered, every accepted call settles, previous valid state survives a failed replacement. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Expose eligible skill metadata and a validated activation path using Schway-native tool/context contracts.
- [ ] Reject model activation of user-only skills; user activation from explicit user invocation still works.
- [ ] Define and document activation scope, replacement/deactivation, and behavior on new session, resume and compaction; persist only semantic activation state if needed, without repeated body copies.
- [ ] Keep skill bodies in dynamic context, separate from ordinary durable messages; preserve project instructions and system overrides.
- [ ] Scripted multi-turn tests verify eligible activation, rejection, failure recovery and lifecycle across compaction/resume without a core workflow engine.
- [ ] All required behavior and verification scenarios above are covered, including failure/cancellation cases relevant to this slice.
- [ ] User-facing commands/configuration and public contracts introduced by this issue are documented with a runnable example where applicable.

title: Run tools from explicitly enabled local TypeScript extensions
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:05 -->

**Milestone:** v0.2
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

A user enables a local TypeScript extension and the agent executes its custom tool through the existing scheduler and validation path. Scope: sections 27–29, 50, 58–59, 79, 90.

## Existing behavior and problem

The existing tool registry already accepts JSON Schema, compiles validators once, rejects duplicate names and exposes parallel/exclusive scheduling. The native ToolContext carries workspace, AbortSignal and streaming output. The missing piece is explicit executable extension loading and a public registration entry point.

## Prerequisite contract

No blockers. Reuse existing tool/runtime contracts and introduce only the small public registration seam needed for this consumer.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Support repeatable --extension <local-module> in interactive and headless startup, preserving explicit argument order. Resolve relative module paths from the primary canonical workspace root; use canonical module identity to reject duplicate enablement.

2. Provide a documented Schway extension entry that receives a capability-limited context with tool registration. Ship an importable public contract from the single package so a packed/installed consumer can typecheck without reaching into private source modules.

3. Invoke extension registration before taking tool definitions for the first model request. JSON Schema remains the public schema type; TypeBox is optional for extension authors.

4. Execute registered tools through the existing validation, AbortSignal, output handling and scheduler. The tool's declared execution mode, not its origin, determines concurrency and barriers. Define and enforce a bounded model-facing result policy for extension returns.

5. Treat extension initialization as atomic: registrations from a module that throws or registers an invalid/duplicate tool must not remain partially active. Fail startup actionably with extension identity; interactive recovery may return to a usable setup state.

6. Disabled or unmentioned modules execute no code. Do not scan dependencies and guess which packages are extensions. Executable extensions are explicitly trusted code; this feature does not claim sandboxing.

7. Preserve core ownership. Extensions register supported capabilities, not replacement loops, sessions, compaction engines, models or schedulers. Public contracts must not require OpenTUI or provider SDK types.

## Scope boundary

Explicit local loading and custom tools. Commands, observers, prompt hooks, package discovery and package installation are separate surfaces.

## Implementation constraints

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
- Schway owns the loop, session engine, context/compaction and tool scheduling. Provider SDKs are protocol clients with automatic retries disabled; core contracts use native conversation types.
- Keep core independent of OpenTUI and provider wire types. Headless execution must not load the TUI; only selected providers and explicitly enabled executable extensions load.
- Resolve tool-relative paths from the canonical primary workspace root (nearest Git root, otherwise launch cwd). Keep runtime events separate from durable semantic session records.
- Document newly exported functions/types with a one-line TSDoc contract. Preserve bounded model-facing output, exactly one result per accepted call and existing credential redaction.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Local TypeScript extension | Installed/headless fixture registers a custom tool and completes a real model → tool → model turn. |
| Scheduling/validation | Invalid arguments never execute; parallel/exclusive declarations and cancellation are honored. |
| Registration failure | Duplicate or invalid tool and thrown initialization leave no half-installed capabilities. |
| Lazy loading | A marker in an unenabled extension is never executed; headless loads no OpenTUI. |
| Package boundary | Public types resolve from a packed consumer; no private path imports are needed. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Provide a small importable extension entry contract and tool registration API, with one-line contract docs and a runnable example.
- [ ] Load only explicitly enabled local modules in deterministic order; support the local extension CLI option in headless and interactive modes.
- [ ] Reuse JSON Schema registration, validation, parallel/exclusive scheduling, bounded results and cancellation; do not require third-party TypeBox.
- [ ] Duplicate names, unsupported schemas and load failures identify the extension and leave a usable failure state.
- [ ] No replacement of agent/session/context/model/scheduler internals; disabled extensions incur no module execution and headless remains TUI-free.
- [ ] An isolated local extension fixture completes a custom-tool conversation through the real loop. Replace obsolete extension absence guards while preserving lazy-load tests.

title: Add extension commands and isolated runtime observers
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:06 -->

**Milestone:** v0.2
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

Enabled extensions add discoverable interactive commands and observe the same runtime events used by headless JSON and the TUI.

## Existing behavior and problem

Explicitly enabled extensions already initialize in a deterministic order and can register custom tools atomically. The TUI currently dispatches fixed built-in slash commands. Runtime events already drive the TUI and headless JSON stream but are not exposed as an isolated extension observation service.

## Prerequisite contract

Requires the explicit extension runtime, source identity, atomic registration and disposal boundary from local extension loading. Existing RuntimeEvent is the canonical event union; additions must serve all consumers.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Extend the public registration context with command registration and runtime-event subscription. Commands declare a name, help description and argument handling; show them in /help and dispatch from the same input editor.

2. Reserve built-in names. Reject conflicts between extension commands and discovered skill commands or other extension commands with both source identities. Registration order must not silently change which command runs.

3. Run registered commands only while the controller is idle; during an active turn show a busy diagnostic and retain input. Command execution can return display text or submit a normal user prompt through a supported controller capability; it cannot take ownership of the loop.

4. Commands that throw produce a source-labelled diagnostic and restore usable editor state. Cancellation and disposal must stop owned asynchronous work through the supplied signal.

5. Observers receive read-only notifications using the existing normalized runtime vocabulary. Protect agent/session state from listener mutation and catch synchronous throws and asynchronous rejections per listener.

6. Observer work must not gate model/tool completion. Preserve delivery order for each listener, bound any queue, and report dropped notifications explicitly if the configured bound is exceeded; authoritative runtime output and durable results remain intact.

7. Return unsubscribe/disposal handles and invoke them when the extension runtime is disposed. Session replacement must not multiply subscriptions or retain handlers for a destroyed controller.

## Scope boundary

Command registration and observation only. Listeners are not intervention hooks, and extension commands do not create a workflow engine.

## Implementation constraints

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
- Schway owns the loop, session engine, context/compaction and tool scheduling. Provider SDKs are protocol clients with automatic retries disabled; core contracts use native conversation types.

- Resolve tool-relative paths from the canonical primary workspace root (nearest Git root, otherwise launch cwd). Keep runtime events separate from durable semantic session records.
- Document newly exported functions/types with a one-line TSDoc contract. Preserve bounded model-facing output, exactly one result per accepted call and existing credential redaction.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Command invocation | Custom help entry and arguments work; submitted prompts use the real controller/loop. |
| Collisions/busy state | Core, skill and extension conflicts are reported; a busy command never mutates an active run. |
| Bad observer | Throw, reject and attempted event mutation do not affect sibling listeners or agent results. |

title: Contribute prompt context and intercept model requests
body:
<!-- schway-roadmap:v03:07 -->

**Milestone:** v0.2
**Planning baseline:** revision `875055e`, package `0.1.0`. Inspect current code before implementation to reuse subsequently landed work. This issue contains its own product requirements and prerequisite contracts; other issue discussions are not required context.

## What to build

An enabled extension can contribute context and influence an agent/model request through the supported beforeAgent, context and beforeModel hooks, without touching provider wire payloads.

## Existing behavior and problem

Schway prepares a stable system prompt plus dynamic context and native conversation items before requesting a model. Local extensions can register capabilities. This ticket adds supported intervention points around that preparation; observation alone cannot implement context contributions or intentional cancellation.

## Prerequisite contract

Requires explicit local extension initialization, deterministic load order and source-labelled registration. Prepared requests contain systemPrompt, named dynamic context, native items, tool descriptions and an AbortSignal; hooks operate on copies of these supported values.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Expose prompt contributions and beforeAgent, context and beforeModel hooks from the enabled extension registration context. Execute hooks in extension load order, awaiting each result before the next hook.

2. beforeAgent runs once per submitted user turn before the first model request and may add turn-scoped context or deny that turn with an explanation. It does not rewrite the durable user message or rerun on a transport retry.

3. context runs after ordinary environment, applicable project instructions, skills and compaction summary are assembled. It returns the next list of dynamic context sections; later hooks see earlier supported changes. Keep named structural sections identifiable.

4. beforeModel sees a native prepared request, may return a transformed ephemeral system/context/conversation view or deny the request, and runs once per logical model request after context preparation. Transport retries reuse that prepared request; a post-compaction overflow recovery prepares a new request and reruns request hooks.

5. Validate hook outputs as Schway-native values. Durable session records and registered tools must remain unmodified; a model-facing tool list can only select registered tool definitions, not invent executable tools or alter their schemas.

6. Specify that internal compaction summarization is not a user-agent turn: these hooks do not recursively intercept its summarizer request. Extension/skill dynamic context is reassembled when the normal model request resumes.

7. Hook throws, rejection or invalid output produce an actionable extension error, stop the affected request safely and leave the process/controller usable. AbortSignal reaches hooks; cleanup must not create unresolved tool calls.

8. Keep provider wire payloads outside the public hook contract. System-prompt override files still affect the base prompt; structural context is assembled before extension interception.

## Scope boundary

The three named lifecycle/request hooks and prompt contributions. No provider-payload mutation, tool interception or replacement of context/compaction ownership.

3. A fork point must be a complete user-turn boundary with all accepted tool calls settled, or the empty conversation root. Reject partial assistant/tool groups, invalid IDs and ambiguous references without changing the active branch.

## What to build

Users explicitly save or remove provider credentials and later run Schway without re-entering keys, using the operating system's secure storage. Scope: sections 63–64, 72–73, 91.

## Existing behavior and problem

API-key resolution currently supports only explicit runtime values and environment variables. Keys are rejected from ordinary configuration. Introduce a third, lower-priority credential source backed by OS-native storage, while preserving deterministic headless behavior and optional/no-auth compatible endpoints.

## Prerequisite contract

No blockers. Reuse existing credential precedence, provider loading and redaction. Export a narrow storage boundary that later subscription auth can use without importing OS details into core.

## Required behavior and decisions

1. Add a credential-store boundary with get/set/delete operations keyed by provider credential identity. Use Bun's available OS-native secure storage behind it; tests inject a fake store and never touch the developer's actual keychain.

2. Resolve credentials in this order: explicit runtime override, environment, secure stored value, missing. An explicitly supplied empty override is an error, not a request to fall back. Read the secure store only if a higher-priority usable source is absent.

3. Provide interactive /login <provider> for masked API-key entry and /logout <provider> to delete that stored credential. Distinguish stored, environment and runtime sources so logout does not claim to remove an environment variable.

4. Derive compatible-provider credential identity from a canonical endpoint or named profile when profiles exist. Native Anthropic/OpenAI identities stay separate. Never reuse a credential across unrelated endpoints by accident.

5. Unavailable, locked or denied secure storage produces an actionable error for save/read/delete. Do not silently fall back to plaintext files. A valid runtime/environment credential remains usable even if the store is unavailable.

6. Keep secret input out of transcript, command recall, configuration, session records and runtime/debug output. Failed/cancelled entry stores nothing; overwrite/delete acts only on the explicitly selected identity.

7. Headless execution may consume existing stored credentials but never initiates interactive login. Optional/none compatible auth continues to work according to its configured mode.

8. Document platform requirements and an opt-in native-store smoke procedure. Do not claim all supported OS stores passed based on a fake-store test.

API keys and secure-store infrastructure. Browser/device OAuth and subscription transport are handled separately; no automatic migration from another CLI.

- Use Bun and TypeScript. Run `bun run typecheck`; run `bun test` for behavior changes. Deterministic checks use scripted models, protocol fixtures and temporary filesystems rather than paid APIs.
